title: Bengaluru Sisters Turn Grandmother's Donne Biryani Into a Rs 10 Crore Business
excerpt: Ramya and Shweta Ravi's RNR Donne Biryani crossed 10,000 orders in its first month in 2020 and has clocked Rs 10 crore since, built on a leaf-pouch Karnataka biryani most of India had never tried.
body:
• Bengaluru sisters Ramya and Shweta Ravi built RNR Donne Biryani on their grandmother's recipe, serving the green, mint-heavy Karnataka biryani in a leaf donne and a tin dabba.
  • The cloud kitchen, launched in 2020 during lockdown, crossed 10,000 orders in its first month, according to The Better India.
  • The sisters say the business has clocked Rs 10 crore in revenue since it began.
  • For diaspora readers, donne biryani is the Bengaluru style most often missing abroad: short-grain rice, mint and meat, sold here with raita, salad and a sweet.

Two Bengaluru sisters have turned a family recipe into a Rs 10 crore food business. Ramya and Shweta Ravi launched RNR Donne Biryani in 2020 to sell the donne biryani they grew up eating at their grandmother's table, according to The Better India.

Donne biryani is Karnataka's own style. It is made with short-grain rice and generous mint, which gives it a green hue, and it is traditionally served in a donne, a pouch made of leaf. Curly Tales notes the style has long lived in the shadow of the Hyderabadi, Lucknowi and Kolkata biryanis.

A Family Already in Food

The sisters did not start cold. Their father runs hotels and restaurants, and both grew up wanting to work in food and hospitality. The lockdown gave them the time to firm up the plan, Ramya told The Better India.

"We wanted to find a way to take that same taste, which we have grown up with, to everyone else."

— Ramya Ravi, co-founder, RNR Donne Biryani

Shweta pointed to the market gap: "The donne biryani sector is unorganised and that is where we saw a business opportunity."

What Makes It Donne

The dish itself is specific. Donne biryani uses flavoursome short-grain rice rather than long basmati, a heavy hand with mint leaves, and tender meat, and it arrives in the leaf pouch that gives it its name, Curly Tales explains. It is a Bengaluru military-hotel staple that stayed local while other regional biryanis went national, which is precisely the gap the sisters set out to close: to popularise what they saw as an underrated gem of a biryani.

Packaging as the Product

Instead of opening a restaurant, the sisters ran a cloud kitchen and spent heavily on presentation. Orders go out in a designed tin dabba with raita, salad and a sweet. "Our idea was to give our customers an unforgettable experience," Ramya said. Alongside the biryani, a drumstick chilly starter and a chicken ghee roast are among the most ordered items.

The model worked quickly. The venture crossed 10,000 orders in its first month of operation, and the sisters say revenue has reached Rs 10 crore since inception.

Why It Travels Well as an Idea

RNR's story is a template diaspora food founders keep reusing: one regional dish, made exactly the family way, sold for delivery first, with the packaging doing the work a dining room would. The dish itself is the marketing. A biryani style that most of India had not heard of became the brand.

What's Next

The sisters say the business is set to keep growing from its Bengaluru base. Whether donne biryani gets the national shelf space Hyderabadi biryani enjoys will depend on whether the cloud-kitchen model can hold quality as orders scale.
